slides.title: Methods for iron determination. Clinical diagnostic significance
bullets: Clinical biochemistry and biochemical testing methods
Practical session — 6 h

slides.title: Lesson outline
bullets: Tests: Serum iron (Fe); Ferritin; Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
Conditions: Iron-deficiency anemia; Hemochromatosis (iron overload)
Reference values: Reference values and decision limits
Practice: Q&A: 8 + 3

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 1/4
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)  ·  Units: µg/dL, µmol/L

What it is used for: Types of iron tests: serum iron (the amount of iron in the blood), transferrin (the protein that moves iron through the body), TIBC — total iron-binding capacity (how well iron attaches to transferrin and other blood proteins) and ferritin (how much iron is stored). Sometimes one test is ordered, sometimes several to understand the results better.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 2/4
bullets: Iron tests are most often used to check whether iron is too low (a sign of anemia, although not everyone with low iron has anemia); diagnose different types of anemia; check whether iron is too high (hemochromatosis, or iron overload, which can be inherited or caused by another condition); measure iron stored in the liver to check for liver disease; check for restless legs syndrome and adult Still disease; and see whether treatment for low or high iron is working.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 3/4
bullets: Symptoms of low iron include weakness or fatigue, dizziness, shortness of breath and arrhythmia. Symptoms of high iron include weakness or fatigue, joint pain (most often in the knees or hands), abdominal pain, loss of interest in sex or erectile dysfunction, and skin that looks gray, metallic or bronze. Low iron may not cause symptoms until it is very low, so a routine test may be ordered.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 4/4
bullets: Physiology: Iron is a mineral the body needs for growth and development. It is used to make hemoglobin, the red blood cell protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to all parts of the body. Iron is also important for healthy muscles, bone marrow and organ function, and for making some hormones. It comes from food or supplements.

Most of the 3 to 4 g of iron in adults is in hemoglobin. Much of the rest is stored as ferritin or hemosiderin in the liver, spleen and bone marrow, or is in muscle myoglobin. Transferrin is the main blood protein that binds and transports iron. The hormone hepcidin is the key regulator of iron absorption and distribution.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: High: If one or more iron tests show high iron, it may mean hemochromatosis, lead poisoning or liver disease.

Low: If one or more iron tests show low iron, it may mean iron deficiency anemia (a common type of anemia), another type of anemia, or thalassemia (an inherited blood disorder in which the body makes fewer healthy red blood cells).

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Low: Conditions that raise the risk of iron-deficiency anemia include blood loss (gastrointestinal bleeding from inflammatory bowel disease, an ulcer, colon cancer or celiac disease; injury or surgery; heavy periods or bleeding in childbirth; regular aspirin or NSAID use; urinary tract bleeding); problems absorbing iron (celiac disease, ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s disease, Helicobacter pylori infection, stomach or intestinal surgery, endurance sports); kidney disease; and long-lasting inflammatory conditions such as congestive heart failure or obesity.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask you to fast for 12 hours before the test, which is usually done in the morning. The amount of iron in the blood varies through the day and may be higher in the morning.

Interferences: Many factors affect serum iron: it rises after each meal, infections and inflammation can lower it, and diurnal variation makes it rise in the morning and fall at night. Its day-to-day variation within a person is greater than that of hemoglobin and hematocrit.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Some medicines, including birth control pills and estrogen treatments, can affect iron levels, and iron may be lower in women during their menstrual cycles. So an abnormal result does not necessarily mean a condition that needs treatment.

Limitations: To understand the result, the provider considers symptoms, age, medical history and other blood tests. Hemoglobin, hematocrit, a complete blood count and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) may also be ordered to check iron levels.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: Each test assesses a different aspect of iron metabolism, so the results of one test may not always agree with another. Lack of standardisation among the tests limits comparison of results between laboratories.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)  ·  Units: ng/mL, µg/L

What it is used for: Ferritin is often ordered as part of a group of iron tests. It helps diagnose or rule out hemochromatosis (iron overload), iron deficiency anemia, liver diseases (much of the body’s ferritin is stored in the liver), restless legs syndrome and adult Still disease; monitor chronic conditions that affect iron (cancer, kidney disease, autoimmune diseases); find low iron before symptoms in people at high risk (being underweight, heavy menstrual bleeding, pregnancy, poor absorption such as with inflammatory bowel disease or after gastrointestinal surgery); and check how well treatment is working.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Serum ferritin is currently the most efficient and cost-effective test for diagnosing iron deficiency. Because it falls during the first stage of iron depletion, it can identify low iron status before anemia develops.

Ordered with symptoms of low iron (shortness of breath, weakness, dizziness, arrhythmia, pale skin, restless legs syndrome) or high iron (weakness, joint pain, loss of interest in sex, abdominal pain, gray, metallic or bronze skin), and when other blood tests show low hematocrit or hemoglobin.
Physiology: Ferritin is a protein that binds to iron and stores it in the body. A ferritin test shows how much iron is stored in the body.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Nearly all ferritin is inside cells; a small amount circulates in the plasma. Under normal conditions serum ferritin is directly related to the amount of stored iron: 1 µg/L of serum ferritin is equivalent to about 10 mg of stored iron.

slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Reference values and decision limits · 1/3
rows: No specific population stated in the source — Inflammation (e.g., with infection) can raise serum ferritin.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Reference values and decision limits · 2/3
rows: Women who test positive for anemia by hemoglobin or hematocrit — Older (1998) guidance: > 15 µg/L suggests iron deficiency is not the cause of the anemia. Newer sources use a different cut-off (see above).

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Reference values and decision limits · 3/3
rows: Apparently healthy adults and children aged 5 and over (pregnancy: first trimester) — Under 5 years the cut-off is <12 µg/L.
Adults and children aged 5 and over with infection or inflammation — Under 5 years the cut-off is <30 µg/L. Conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: High: Higher than normal ferritin can be caused by too much iron in the body. Other causes include inflammation (for example, from infection or surgery), an autoimmune disorder, liver disease, cancer, obesity, alcohol use disorder and hyperthyroidism.
High: A high ferritin level is typical in people who have hemochromatosis. Ferritin tests are also used to see whether iron levels are improving with treatment.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Low: Lower than normal ferritin may mean iron deficiency anemia or another condition related to low iron. Without treatment, iron deficiency anemia can lead to heart problems, infections, and slow growth and brain development in children.

Low: Iron deficiency develops in stages: 1) storage iron depletion — serum ferritin and bone marrow iron decrease; 2) iron-deficient erythropoiesis — stores are depleted and transferrin saturation declines, but hemoglobin is usually normal; 3) iron deficiency anemia — hemoglobin and hematocrit fall and red cells are small with little hemoglobin (microcytic, hypochromic anemia).

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask you to fast for 12 hours before the test, which is usually done in the morning.

Interferences: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: chronic infection, inflammation or diseases that damage tissues and organs (hepatitis, cirrhosis, neoplasia, arthritis) can raise it independent of iron status. This rise can mask depleted iron stores.
Certain medicines can decrease or increase ferritin levels; an abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: WHO (2020) recommends assessing ferritin together with two acute-phase proteins, CRP and AGP, where infection or inflammation is widespread; with inflammation the iron-deficiency cut-off is raised (adults <70 µg/L, children under 5 <30 µg/L).

Limitations: Anemia of chronic disease (anemia of inflammation) can be difficult to diagnose: although low serum ferritin indicates iron deficiency, ferritin tends to be higher with infection or inflammation. In this anemia, inflammatory cytokines raise hepcidin and iron is diverted from the circulation to storage sites.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: In the anaemia algorithm ferritin is the first test in microcytic (low MCV) anaemia: a low ferritin confirms iron deficiency; with normal or high ferritin, anaemia of chronic disease (inflammation), thalassaemia and other causes are considered. Full path: Learn → Tables and algorithms → Anaemia.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)  ·  Units: µg/dL, µmol/L, g/L, %
What it is used for: When hemochromatosis is suspected, doctors may check levels of iron and transferrin, the ratio of iron to transferrin, and ferritin.

Physiology: Transferrin is the protein that moves iron throughout the body; a transferrin test measures it. TIBC (total iron-binding capacity) measures how well iron attaches to transferrin and other proteins in the blood.
TIBC reflects the availability of iron-binding sites on transferrin: it increases when serum iron (and stored iron) is low and decreases when they are high.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Transferrin saturation shows the extent to which transferrin has vacant iron-binding sites (low saturation means a high proportion of vacant sites). It is calculated from two measurements: transferrin saturation (%) = serum iron (µg/dL) / TIBC (µg/dL) × 100. Saturation is highest in newborns, decreases by age 4 months, and then increases through childhood and adolescence to adult levels.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Reference values and decision limits
rows: Transferrin saturation: used to confirm iron deficiency
Adults — CDC (1998). Among non-pregnant women of childbearing age, sensitivity 20% and specificity 93% (against absent stainable bone-marrow iron).

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: High: A high ratio of iron to transferrin (transferrin saturation) may suggest hemochromatosis. The CDC report (1998) describes transferrin saturation as the recommended screening test for hemochromatosis: a repeated high value indicates hemochromatosis.

Low: A transferrin saturation of less than 16% among adults is often used to confirm iron deficiency. Saturation indicates iron-deficient erythropoiesis rather than iron depletion, so it is less sensitive to changes in iron stores than serum ferritin.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Low: In iron-deficient erythropoiesis (marginal, mild functional deficiency), iron stores are depleted and transferrin saturation declines, but hemoglobin is usually still within the normal range.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask you to fast for 12 hours before the test, which is usually done in the morning.

Interferences: Inflammation, chronic infection, malignancies, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome and malnutrition can lower TIBC, while oral contraceptives and pregnancy can raise it. Even so, its day-to-day variation is less than that of serum iron.

Factors that affect serum iron and TIBC — iron status, diurnal variation and day-to-day variation — also affect transferrin saturation; its diurnal variation is larger than that of hemoglobin or hematocrit.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: TIBC is less sensitive to iron deficiency than serum ferritin, because changes in TIBC occur only after iron stores are depleted.

Read iron tests together: in iron deficiency serum iron and transferrin saturation are low, TIBC is usually high and ferritin is low; in anaemia of inflammation (chronic disease) iron and TIBC are low while ferritin may be normal or high. Dolgov et al. cite the soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR), which changes little with inflammation, to tell the two apart.

slides.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
bullets: Diagnosis uses a complete blood count, hemoglobin, blood iron and ferritin; in iron-deficiency anemia iron and ferritin are low. The cause is also sought: gastrointestinal bleeding, heavy periods, surgery, aspirin/NSAID use and others.

slides.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
rows: Complete blood count: hemoglobin, red cells, hematocrit, MCV
Red cell count, hemoglobin, hematocrit or MCV outside the normal range may signal anemia.
Shows how much iron is stored in the body; low in iron-deficiency anemia.
The amount of iron in the blood; low in iron-deficiency anemia.

slides.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
rows: The iron-carrying protein (transferrin) and how well iron attaches to it (TIBC).
Finding the cause: stool blood testing, colonoscopy or endoscopy help find a source of bleeding.
Monitoring whether treatment works; oral iron often takes 3–6 months to restore iron levels.

slides.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
rows: Iron-deficiency anemia is likely; the cause (blood loss and others) is sought.
Possible iron-deficiency anemia, another type of anemia, or thalassemia.
Ferritin <15 µg/L (healthy adults) or <70 µg/L (with inflammation)
Iron deficiency per WHO (2020); CRP (and AGP) are measured to assess inflammation.
Heterogeneous microcytosis typical of iron deficiency; confirm with ferritin and transferrin saturation.

slides.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
bullets: Birth control pills and estrogen affect iron levels; levels may be lower during menstruation. Iron is higher in the morning — the test is usually done in the morning after a 12-hour fast.

slides.title: Hemochromatosis (iron overload)
bullets: Too much iron builds up in the body. Diagnosis is based on medical and family history, a physical exam, blood tests and sometimes a liver biopsy.

slides.title: Hemochromatosis (iron overload)
rows: Iron studies: blood iron, transferrin and ferritin, and the ratio of iron to transferrin.
A high iron-to-transferrin ratio may suggest hemochromatosis.
A high ferritin level is typical of hemochromatosis.
Checks for the gene mutations that cause hemochromatosis.

slides.title: Hemochromatosis (iron overload)
rows: Ferritin may be checked during treatment to see whether iron levels are improving.

slides.title: Hemochromatosis (iron overload)
rows: Hemochromatosis is possible — clarified with genetic testing.
With raised transferrin saturation and ferritin, supports HFE hemochromatosis; penetrance is incomplete, so the clinician concludes together with evidence of iron overload.
Possible hemochromatosis, lead poisoning or liver disease.

slides.title: Hemochromatosis (iron overload)
bullets: A liver biopsy may be used to confirm iron overload, rule out other liver diseases and show scarring.

slides.title: A patient with an active infection has a normal ferritin. Does this prove iron stores are adequate?
options: No, inflammation can raise ferritin and mask low stores
Yes, a normal ferritin always proves stores are adequate
Yes, because infection only lowers ferritin
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. That is why ferritin is interpreted with other markers during inflammation.

Basis: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: inflammation raises it regardless of iron status and can mask depleted stores.

slides.title: Serum iron is 9.0 µmol/L (50 µg/dL) and TIBC is 71.6 µmol/L (400 µg/dL). What is the transferrin saturation?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. This is below the 16% cut-off used in adults to confirm iron deficiency.

Basis: Transferrin saturation (%) = serum iron / TIBC × 100 = 50 / 400 × 100 = 12.5%.

The following forms of erythrocytes were found in a peripheral blood smear: macrocytes, megalocytes, erythrocytes with Howell-Jolly bodies and Cabot rings, poikilocytosis. Which anemia can be suspected:
A patient developed signs of anemia three years after gastric resection. Blood test: RBC 2.3×10¹²/L, Hb 92 g/L, color index 1.2, macro- and megalocytosis. Which anemia can be suspected:
Anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
bullets: 1. Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is the most common anemia; causes: chronic blood loss (menorrhagia in women, GI bleeding), increased demand (pregnancy, growth), malabsorption (celiac disease, gastrectomy, H. pylori), inadequate dietary intake.
2. Stages: first the stores are depleted (ferritin↓), then iron delivery is impaired (TSAT↓, CHr↓), and finally Hb falls – Hb is a late sign.

3. Laboratory criteria: ferritin <30 ng/mL or TSAT <20% – absolute iron deficiency (StatPearls); AGA/ASH recommend ferritin <45 ng/mL for IDA; WHO 2020: <15 µg/L in healthy adults, <70 µg/L in infection/inflammation; serum iron varies through the day and is unreliable alone.

slides.title: Anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
bullets: 4. Blood: microcytic hypochromic anemia, RDW↑, anisopoikilocytosis, "pencil" cells, target cells; reticulocytes low/normal; thrombocytosis may occur.
5. Differentiation: thalassemia trait (ferritin normal, RDW often normal, Hb electrophoresis), anemia of chronic disease (ferritin normal/high), sideroblastic anemia.
6. Response to treatment: 1–2 weeks after iron is given, reticulocytes rise, then Hb; looking for the cause (source of bleeding) is mandatory.

slides.title: Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
bullets: 1. Peripheral blood: Hb decreased, MCV <80 fL, MCH and MCHC low (hypochromia), RDW increased; the smear shows microcytes, anisopoikilocytosis, elliptocytes ("pencil" cells), target cells.
2. Reticulocytes normal or low (absolute count low), CHr/Ret-He <28 pg; platelets often normal or reactively increased.

3. Bone marrow (rarely needed for diagnosis): erythroid hyperplasia, predominance of small early erythroid cells with "ragged" cytoplasm; with Perls stain (Prussian blue) there is no iron in macrophages and sideroblasts are sharply reduced.

slides.title: Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
bullets: 4. Bone marrow iron is the gold standard for assessing stores, but invasive; in practice replaced by ferritin and TSAT.
5. Differentiation: in anemia of chronic disease, iron in bone marrow macrophages is preserved/increased; in sideroblastic anemia – ring sideroblasts.

slides.title: Iron metabolism. The role of transferrin, ferritin, hepcidin?
bullets: 1. Iron absorption in the duodenum: dietary Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺ and enters the enterocyte; basolateral exit via ferroportin, then it is oxidized and binds to transferrin.
2. Transferrin carries iron in the blood and delivers it to cells via transferrin receptors; TIBC is the total iron-binding capacity of transferrin, TSAT = serum iron/TIBC.
3. Ferritin is the intracellular iron storage protein; serum ferritin reflects stores (low – deficiency), but as an acute-phase protein it rises in inflammation.

slides.title: Iron metabolism. The role of transferrin, ferritin, hepcidin?
bullets: 4. Hepcidin is a liver hormone that degrades ferroportin: with iron excess and in inflammation (IL-6) it rises, reducing absorption and release from macrophages; in deficiency and hypoxia it falls.
5. Clinical reflection: iron deficiency (ferritin↓, TSAT↓, transferrin↑), anemia of inflammation (ferritin normal/↑, TSAT↓, hepcidin↑), iron overload/hemochromatosis (TSAT and ferritin↑).
